caption:
Who is suffering from your refusal to pursue your purpose?

Odysseus spent ten years trying to get home, and the whole time Ithaca was falling apart without him. Penelope was holding off a house full of men who wanted her land. Telemachus grew up guessing at what a father was supposed to be. The kingdom didn’t pause and wait politely while he finished his journey. It paid for every year he wasn’t there.

We talk about purpose like it’s a personal luxury, something you get to once the bills are handled and the kids are older and the timing finally feels safe. But the fully expressed version of you is somebody else’s proof that it’s possible. The people who need the exact thing you’re carrying are sitting in a house you haven’t come home to yet, and they don’t know your name, so they can’t come find you.

The delay is never neutral. Your subconscious is running a program that says staying small is safer than being seen, and until you rewrite it you’ll keep taking the long way home.

If you’re ready to step into your purpose and want guidance on how to start, you can start with the tools in my bio or book a 1:1 breakthrough session with me. 

Your dreams are destined. But it’s up to you to pursue them in this life or not.

author: Destiny | Subconscious Reprogramming & Mindset
transcript: And the thing nobody tells you about purpose is that your avoidance of it has a body count. In the Odyssey, there's a bow that only Odysseus can string. All the strongest suitors take turns and not one of them can do it because it was never a contest of strength. It was a matter of purpose. Some things are made for one set of hands and if those hands don't show up, the consequences come with a body count, whether literally or figuratively, of all the people who needed your gift but never got to receive it. And you already know what yours is. That's the uncomfortable part. You've known since you were young, as a feeling and a thought and a dream that you keep coming back to no matter what. It's that thing you avoid because maybe you don't feel good enough or it doesn't feel safe enough to pursue. So you choose the safer path, the one that feels more comfortable, less risky, or more likely to feed your ego in a way that makes you feel good or look good to others. Just as Odysseus went off to fight someone else's war in Troy. And yes, he did become the legendary hero who won the war but at what cost? His home is like a withered, his house filled with men eating his food, abusing his family, kicking his dog and trying to take over by marrying his wife. And all of his men who died along the way, that was the cost of strain from his purpose and his own morality. The wrong path, no matter how glorious it looks in the beginning, gets more dangerous the longer you stay on it. Until all his men had died and he washed up on his shore, having forgotten his original journey in the first place. And isn't that the trap that happens to so many of us? We tell ourselves we'll come back to our goals and dreams, and sometimes get so swept off the path on the thing that looks good to the rest of the world. And then end up so far from the original goal that it feels impossible, or like we've forgotten it all together. But you never really forget, do you? Odysseus spent seven years on an island with Calypso, the goddess who offered him immortality. And still he sat on the shore every day and wept, trying to put his boat back together without even knowing why. And that's the pull that never goes away when it comes to our purpose. It's the reason you can be doing well, being paid, being praised. You can be seemingly successful inside someone else's path, and you'll still feel that ache. That never quite happy, never quite satisfied, never quite enough ache. Because that path was never meant for you to stay on, and you will always be called towards your Dharma in this life. Comfort is not the same as alignment. Only when Odysseus was ready to surrender to the fear of Poseidon's punishment, the fear of failure, of ego death, of perhaps returning to a disappointing truth, or to people who were disappointed in him, only when he surrendered and let the ocean take him, did he finally end up back home in a place where his bow and his people were always waiting for him to strain the bow that was only meant for him to string. So let me ask you, what is your bow, and who is suffering every day you refuse to string it?
title: Your Purpose Avoidance Has a Body Count
one_liner: Avoiding your purpose doesn't just hurt you — it costs everyone who needed your unique gift.
key_points: The Odyssey's bow symbolizes that some roles are meant for one person — if you don't show up, real harm follows
Choosing a safer, ego-flattering path (like Odysseus fighting Troy) pulls you further from your true purpose over time
Even amid success and praise, straying from your purpose creates a persistent ache that never fully goes away
Surrendering to fear of failure is often the exact moment you finally return to what you were meant to do
